items.title: Societal Expectations for AI Deployments in Policing
items.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) by police forces remains a contentious topic. While citizens expect police forces to have the knowledge and resources to fight crimes effectively, the usage of AI by police forces raises legitimate concerns about biases, chilling effects and accountability in case of errors. This chapter provides insights into the level of societal acceptance and trust in the police use of AI, based on a national citizen consultation of 10,114 citizens in the United Kingdom. The consultation demonstrates a considerable level of public acceptance and trust but also identifies demographic and personal factors that impact acceptance and trust levels. items.abstract: Accountability for artificial intelligence (AI) in security and policing depends on coordinated decisions, evidence and review across organisational roles and throughout the AI lifecycle. This chapter examines the AI Accountability in Policing and Security (AIPAS) tool, an access-controlled workspace for assessing and evidencing accountability for a specific AI capability and use context. AIPAS organises questions around twelve accountability principles and eight practical themes, links answers and rationales to evidence and change records and supports role-based collaboration. The ‘Knowledge Base’ retrieves passages from AIPAS guidance, the ‘Check Assistant’ flags incomplete or inconsistent free text and the ‘Template Editor’ manages approved changes to the question set. Project spaces and reports help authorised teams review progress and evidence. The chapter also defines responsibilities that remain with operational, technical, legal, oversight, security and communications functions. AIPAS is available through controlled access for security and policing organisations; it does not determine lawfulness, proportionality or deployment decisions and cannot transfer human or organisational accountability to software.

items.title: Spatial Memory Intelligence: Endowing World Models with Understanding-Driven Long-Term Memory
items.abstract: Long-video generation and world models have shown strong potential for interactive entertainment and embodied simulation by predicting future observations conditioned on user actions and historical memory. However, as memory sequences grow longer and their structures become increasingly complex, managing long-range spatial context becomes increasingly challenging, calling for a more intelligent and systematic memory-management strategy. Building on the advancing spatial reasoning capabilities of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and the broader vision of unified models, we propose Spatial Memory Intelligence (SMI), the first framework to systematically employ an understanding model for spatial-memory management in long-video world models. SMI introduces four coordinated atomic operations: spatial clustering, within-cluster sparsification, action-aware retrieval, and reliability-aware filtering. Extensive experiments across multiple baselines, benchmarks, and world-model backbones demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of SMI, achieving comprehensive improvements in memory sparsity, generation stability, and spatial consistency.

items.title: SpectraDL: A Historical Issue-Driven, Test Specification-Assisted Transfer Testing Approach for Deep Learning Frameworks via LLMs
items.abstract: Deep learning (DL) frameworks provide diverse fundamental algorithmic units as operators, which are critical infrastructure for constructing various intelligent software. Since mainstream frameworks widely adopt the open-source development paradigm, bugs may recur across operators and even across frameworks. Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) and historical issues to generate cross-framework test cases. However, existing approaches still suffer from two limitations. First, their test cases have low fault detection capability because they mainly reuse inputs or contexts from historical issues without considering the underlying root causes. Second, an effective mechanism for determining the appropriate transfer scope within a target framework is lacking. To overcome these limitations, we propose SpectraDL, a historical issue-driven, test specification-assisted transfer testing approach for DL frameworks. SpectraDL first extracts rigorous test specifications for each operator from official documentation, and then extracts and transforms historical issues and associated pull requests into structured fault representations (i.e., bug patterns). SpectraDL uses a dual retrieval mechanism based on semantic intent and structural input-space features to transfer these bug patterns to related operators across frameworks. Experiments on four mainstream DL frameworks show that SpectraDL detected 125 previously unknown bugs, 107 of which developers confirmed. The results confirm that SpectraDL delivers a promising transfer testing approach for DL frameworks.

items.title: SPHERE: Adaptive VR Indoor Scene Generation via LLM-Enhanced Spatial Preference Learning and Human-in-the-Loop RL
items.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) advance 3D indoor scene synthesis, current pipelines fail to retain user-specific preferences across sessions, making immersive authoring a repetitive and physically fatiguing process. We present SPHERE, an adaptive VR generation framework that transforms isolated synthesis into continuous human-AI co-creation. SPHERE extracts persistent spatial preferences from natural multimodal interactions (speech and controller edits). To ensure geometric resilience against spatial distortions, it abstracts these raw edits into hierarchical constraints modeling both local functional and global topological contexts. Furthermore, a human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning mechanism dynamically updates retrieval policies based on the user's final edited scenes. A mixed-design user study ($N=42$) and an offline ablation demonstrate that SPHERE significantly reduces corrective edits and physical demand, preventing bias toward shallow object-level traits to yield geometrically resilient, profile-aligned layouts. Ultimately, SPHERE demonstrates how capturing demonstrated spatial logic enables controlled spatial adaptation, establishing a reliable, governed human-AI collaboration framework for immersive authoring. Project page and source code will be available at: https://github.com/hyeonmin11/SPHERE

items.title: Spiking neural transformer based confidentiality preserving framework for breast cancer detection in histopathology images
items.abstract: Breast cancer diagnosis by medical imaging requires accuracy and high sensitivity to patient information. Even though artificial intelligence has made major progress in the field of histopathological image analysis, there are still limitations such as noise in the image, structural variability, and class imbalance, low interpretability of deep learning models, high computational complexity, and privacy risks. To overcome these limitations, this paper suggests a Confidentiality-Preserving Spiking Neural Transformer for Breast Cancer Detection (CP-SNT) to secure and robustly detect breast cancer. In initial phase Robust Double-Weighted Guided Image Filtration (RDWGIF) is applied to improve the quality of histopathological images and reduce noise, but not fine tissue borders. This is followed by the Discrete Quaternion Quadratic Phase Fourier Transform (DQQPFT) that obtains discriminative frequency and phase-domain features, allowing the representation of complex structural and textual patterns. The central classification layer is a Probabilistic Spiking Neural Network (PSNN) that is integrated with a Causality-Aware Transformer Network (CATN) spike-based uncertainty modeling and attention-directed learning, respectively. To maintain the privacy of data in training and inference, PrivTuner using Homomorphic Encryption allows the safe computation of medical data encrypted with the homomorphic encryption to avoid the disclosure of sensitive patient data. The proposed CP-SNT framework is evaluated on the publicly available BreakHis and Breast Histopathology Images (BHI) datasets of 16,116 images to validate classification performance across multi-scale and patch-level histopathological samples. Comprehensive experimental validation on the BreakHis and BHI datasets demonstrates that the proposed CP-SNT model achieves accuracies of 98.60% and 98.37%, respectively. The framework further records precision values above 98.1% and F1-scores near 98.2%, reflecting its strong capability to minimize both false positives and false negatives. Such outstanding performance highlights the effectiveness of the hybrid spiking-transformer architecture combined with encrypted-domain computation for secure and high-confidence breast cancer diagnosis.

items.title: SPONGE: Adaptive Boundary-Anchored Indexing for Online Value-Flow Queries
items.abstract: The application of high-precision value-flow analysis is experiencing a paradigm shift from planned executions to online ad hoc queries driven by human auditors and AI agents. However, existing techniques struggle in this interactive setting: exhaustive offline tabulation is fundamentally intractable, while memoryless online search suffers from redundant exploration and SMT invocations. To bridge this gap, we propose SPONGE, a novel two-phase framework that accelerates ad hoc queries through boundary-anchored indexing. Offline, SPONGE employs an adaptive-depth strategy to selectively precompute feasible value-flow segments at critical procedure boundaries, optimizing SMT allocation based on traversal probability and search space complexity. Online, it utilizes an index-guided push-down search with lazy expansion to dynamically stitch these pre-verified segments, effectively bypassing redundant state exploration and pruning unsatisfiable paths. We evaluated SPONGE on 9 C/C++ projects (up to 3.8 million LoC). Results demonstrate that SPONGE drops the 95th-percentile online query time from nearly 270 s to under 50 s compared to a baseline search. Furthermore, the adaptive strategy reduces offline indexing time by 75% over a uniform approach, amortizing the offline cost in fewer than 300 queries for workloads dominated by complex queries.

items.title: Spontaneity and authorship: a Kantian account of human authorship in copyright law
items.abstract: Generative AI has revived a neglected question in copyright law: why must authors be human? Courts and copyright offices have largely answered through statutory interpretation, but the underlying jurisprudence remains underdeveloped. This article draws on Kant’s theory of publication and spontaneity to argue that copyright protects an imputable communicative act. A copyright work transcends its status as a produced object to exist fundamentally as a public address attributable to a rational subject capable of authorising its communication. The article grounds this account in the architecture of Kant’s Doctrine of Right: the mandate that authorises publication is a relation between persons, modelled on the Roman mandatum, and the standing from which it issues is an exercise of the author’s innate right of communicative freedom. Current AI systems possess the capacity to generate outputs, yet they remain incapable of originating communicative acts or issuing mandates in the Kantian sense. The article further develops a Mandate Test for human-AI collaboration and concludes that the human authorship requirement follows from the nature of authorship itself, not merely from historical practice or legislative convention.

items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To examine within-company associations of occupational health professional staffing and coordinating structure for Health and Productivity Management (HPM) promotion with the HPM implementation score. METHODS: We analyzed an unbalanced panel of 3,966 companies (9,440 company-year observations) for fiscal years 2021-2023. The outcome was a relative HPM implementation score standardized among responding companies. Company fixed-effects models included staffing [ln(n + 1)], coordinating structure, fiscal-year fixed effects, ln-transformed employee count, and company-clustered robust standard errors. RESULTS: Occupational health professional staffing was positively associated with the HPM implementation score (coefficient, 1.028, 95% CI 0.540-1.515, P<0.001). Other coordinating-structure categories had lower scores than an independent dedicated department (coefficients, -0.813 to -5.314; 95% CIs, -1.418 to -0.208 and -6.884 to -3.745; all P ≤ 0.008). CONCLUSIONS: Both factors were associated with HPM implementation within companies over time.

items.title: Starry Textscapes: Astronomy, Cultural Memory, and AI in Language and Literature A Critical Review
items.abstract: This critical review examines the underexplored convergence of astronomical cultural memory and artificial intelligence in literary studies. Drawing on scholarship in cultural astronomy, memory studies, and AI literary analysis, it argues that both the night sky and algorithmic systems function as memory technologies that organize, transmit, and transform cultural narratives. Traditional constellation lore, from Mesopotamian, East Asian, and Indigenous traditions to medieval European literature has historically encoded cosmic order, social hierarchy, and collective identity into narrative form. Simultaneously, large language models have emerged as generative agents that destabilize authorship and introduce probabilistic mechanisms of textual production. Despite substantial activity in each domain, existing research treats them largely in isolation. To address this gap, the review proposes the concept of Celestial Algorithmic Memory (CAM), a tripartite framework of encoding, transformation, and reception that theorizes how astronomical narratives are digitized, statistically reproduced, and reinterpreted under algorithmic conditions. Methodologically, the study synthesizes peer-reviewed literature (2010–2026) through a systematic search strategy adapted from PRISMA-P principles. Findings highlight persistent divergences between human and AI-generated narratives in emotional depth, moral ambiguity, and cultural specificity, while underscoring the political stakes of training-data selection. The review concludes that as AI increasingly mediates literary production, critical attention to whose celestial narratives are preserved, mutated, or erased becomes an ethical as well as scholarly imperative. CAM thus offers an integrated lens for future interdisciplinary inquiry at the intersection of cultural astronomy, memory studies, and critical AI literary analysis.

items.title: Strategic leadership for agentic AI in education: a conceptual framework with reference to the United Arab Emirates
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) shifts educational leadership from whether to adopt a tool to which actions a configured system may take, under whose authority, and with what capacity for intervention and remedy. Through critical integrative synthesis of educational leadership, organisational decision-making, AI governance, and agentic-AI scholarship, this Conceptual Analysis develops educational agentic alignment: a relational judgement about whether delegated machine authority fits educational purposes, human decision rights, professional capabilities, safeguards, pedagogy, and public-value obligations. The focal unit is a dated and versioned educational delegation arrangement. The framework separates agentic capability, use-related exposure, and usable governance capacity; organises leadership decisions through seven domains across four levels; and proposes three mechanisms concerning safeguard shortfall, responsibility–capacity mismatch, and evidence-linked realignment. Each proposition specifies the analytical unit, variables, expected direction, measurable outcomes, time order, moderators, rivals, and evidence that would count against it. Official evidence from the United Arab Emirates illustrates contextual boundaries without implying national implementation or framework validation. The contribution is an education-specific explanation of fit and misfit in human–machine authority, together with a practical basis for bounded decisions and comparative research.

items.title: Student-Guided Teacher Distillation for Efficient LLM Task Routing: Positioning Against Jev-Style System-1 Classifiers
items.abstract: Zero-shot classifiers are useful for routing user requests to specialized LLM tasks, but scoring every request against a large candidate set is expensive: a zero-shot NLI classifier must evaluate one premise-hypothesis pair per label, so cost scales linearly with taxonomy size. We study a student-guided teacher distillation pipeline for a fixed taxonomy of 60 LLM task categories: a compact ModernBERT classifier predicts the full category distribution in one forward pass and retrieves a small top-k candidate set, and a larger DeBERTa-v3 zero-shot NLI classifier reranks only those candidates rather than all 60 labels; the resulting teacher labels iteratively improve the student, which produces sharper candidates for the next round. Unlike generic embedding retrieval or clustering-derived shortlists used in extreme multi-label classification, our candidate generator is trained end-to-end on the target taxonomy and is the same model serving production traffic, distinguishing it from LLM-routing work that routes between candidate models, and from concurrent System-1 encoder-classifier proposals (e.g. TypeSafe AI's Jev and the open-source Laya project) whose training methodology is undocumented or RL-based. Our best student checkpoint reaches 77.5% teacher agreement on a 200-example evaluation set, and preliminary coverage measurements show Coverage@16 of 91-100%, suggesting top-k sets retain most of the teacher's decision-relevant information. items.title: Students' Perception and Use of AI Chatbots as Learning Companions: A Study of Mass Communication Postgraduate Students of Caleb University
items.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly AI-powered and generative AI chatbots, has transformed the ways students access information, obtain academic assistance, and engage with learning activities. This study examined the perception of AI chatbots as learning companions among Mass Communication postgraduate students at Caleb University, Lagos State. Specifically, the study determined students’ level of awareness and understanding of AI chatbots, identified their academic uses, examined their perceptions and attitudes, and assessed the perceived benefits and challenges associated with their use. The study was anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 40 Mass Communication postgraduate students of Caleb University during the 2025/2026 academic session, while total enumeration sampling was used to include the entire population. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire administered electronically via Google Forms and analysed using frequency and percentage statistics. Findings revealed a high level of awareness and understanding of AI chatbots among the students. However, the study also identified challenges including overdependence, reduced academic effort, inaccurate information, inadequate verification, and possible effects on critical thinking. The study concludes that AI chatbots can provide valuable academic support when used responsibly, critically, and as complementary tools rather than substitutes for students’ independent learning and intellectual effort.

items.title: Supportive AI in Mental Health Clinical Text, Screening, Conversational Support, and Documentation in Latin America
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is being studied in mental health for text analysis, assisted screening, structured conversational interventions, risk prediction, and documentation. The dominant evidence stage remains retrospective development, early evaluation, or short studies in selected populations. Evidence is relatively more developed for natural-language processing, text classification, and structured chatbots targeting depression or anxiety symptoms. Supervised generative documentation is an emerging opportunity whose operational risk may be bounded through human review, not a clinically validated capability. Overall, external validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation remain limited or heterogeneous. The evidence does not support independent diagnosis, unsupervised generative therapy, reliable individual suicide prediction, or automated crisis management. Selected studies from Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Chile support preliminary transferability, retrospective prediction, feasibility, or bounded evaluation, not regional effectiveness or implementation readiness. Cultural and linguistic bias, privacy, crisis escalation, and human accountability are design requirements. Current defensible uses are limited to reviewable support with bounded risk; applications that may alter diagnosis, treatment, or crisis response require a prior research agenda and clinical and institutional approval. This is a narrative community evidence brief, not a formal scoping review or clinical guideline.

items.title: Supportive AI in Pediatrics Clinical Decision-Making, Imaging, Critical Care, and Documentation Workflows in Latin America
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in pediatrics has visible evidence in clinical decision support, radiology, neonatal and pediatric intensive care, asthma, pediatric surgery, medication safety, and clinical-text processing. The dominant evidence stage remains retrospective development and early evaluation. External validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation are less common. Models trained in adults or in health systems with different data, infrastructure, and epidemiology cannot be transferred to children in Latin America without local evaluation. Age, weight, maturation, family context, consent, assent, and longitudinal development affect both performance and consequences of error. The regional corpus includes a Brazilian narrative review, a COVID-19 mortality prediction study from Brazil, a PAHO information-systems framework, and studies of retinopathy-of- prematurity screening and neonatal mortality. The three primary studies demonstrate model development and technical evaluation, not clinical utility, impact, or Latin American generalizability. The most defensible current uses are information reading and prioritization, supervised support for repetitive tasks with bounded risk, and reviewable drafts. Predictive applications in critical care, dosing, and deterioration require a prior research agenda with subgroup validation, a defined human response, stopping criteria, and clinical and institutional approval before any prospective protocol. items.title: SWE-PDB: Teaching LLMs to Leverage Debugging Tools via Agentic Training
items.abstract: Interaction with debugging tools enables large language models (LLMs) to reason over concrete runtime states, rather than relying solely on static analysis of source code. Specifically, with the help of a debugger, an LLM-based agent can observe actual program execution by inspecting intermediate variable states and stepping through the control flow. These runtime observations enable the model to better understand program behavior and identify the root causes of bugs. Despite these advantages, using debuggers correctly and effectively remains challenging for many models because debugger interaction is inherently stateful and requires executing complex, long-horizon action sequences. As a result, models often exhibit unproductive interactions in which the debugger is underutilized or even disrupts the debugging process. To address this challenge, we propose SWE-PDB , the first training-based framework that teaches LLMs to leverage debuggers for interactive debugging and program repair. Our approach constructs large-scale buggy Python instances with verified failing tests from diverse sources and synthesizes multi-turn interactive debugging trajectories that follow structured debugging workflows. To ensure data quality, we apply multi-stage trajectory filtering and refinement, and train models using agentic supervised fine-tuning to learn effective debugger behaviors, followed by agentic reinforcement learning with rule-based rewards to improve generalization and promote more strategic debugger usage. Extensive evaluations across diverse benchmarks demonstrate substantial gains. In particular, SWE-PDB-14B achieves 38.0% accuracy on SWE-bench Verified with complete test suites, more than tripling the base model’s performance, while improving interaction efficiency and exhibiting robust, meaningful debugger usage.

items.title: Synthesizing Graph Queries from Demonstrations
items.abstract: Writing graph queries is challenging for non-experts due to the complexity of graph data models and the need to identify proper graph patterns. While recent research has advanced query synthesis for relational and document databases, the problem of synthesizing graph queries remains under-explored. We present a novel approach for synthesizing graph queries from computation demonstrations, where users specify the desired output through expressions over properties of input graphs. Our method addresses the challenge of inferring meaningful graph patterns for matching and efficiently constructing the remaining components of the query. Specifically, we combine graph mining, which identifies candidate patterns across input graphs, with deduction-based pruning, which guides an efficient synthesis of the filtering predicate and return clause. We have implemented our approach in a tool called DMiner and evaluated it on 90 benchmarks. Experimental results show that DMiner successfully synthesizes desired queries for 87 benchmarks, with an average synthesis time of 0.6 seconds per query. This outperforms both enumerative search and LLM baselines. We also conducted a user study, which shows that users can provide demonstrations with modest effort and 87.5% of the provided demonstrations are sufficient for DMiner to synthesize the desired query.

items.title: TACO: Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse Optimizer for LLM Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: Full-parameter fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) incurs substantial optimizer state memory overhead, limiting the model sizes that fit on modern GPUs. Existing approaches either compress optimizer state, abandon first-order gradients, or change the update geometry while retaining dense state. The recently introduced Muon optimizer reduces optimizer memory through matrix-valued updates. Still, its geometry differs from AdamW and can lead to performance degradation when fine-tuning AdamW-pretrained models. To reduce optimizer memory without sacrificing accuracy or computational efficiency in LLM fine-tuning, we propose Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse optimizer, or TACO, which follows Muon's operator-norm steepest-descent view but takes the geometric route further. TACO computes the exact steepest-descent direction under a dimension-normalized $1\to1$ operator norm by selecting the sign of the largest magnitude entry in each column of two-dimensional weight matrices. This retains first-order gradients while making optimizer state memory nearly negligible. Our practical TACO optimizer maintains only a small set of low precision gradient components per column, reducing persistent optimizer state by $174\times$ relative to AdamW8bit (from 27.7 GB to 0.16 GB) and peak training memory by $2.9\times$ (from 80.6 GB to 27.5 GB) on OPT-13B, while achieving comparable accuracy and runtime. TACO further enables full-parameter fine-tuning of 30-32B-parameter models on a single 80 GB H100 GPU across multiple model families and tasks.

items.title: TACOMORE: Exploring a replicable prompting protocol for LLM-assisted corpus analysis
items.abstract: As the data available to corpus linguistics continues to scale ever upwards, researchers are facing a growing methodological bottleneck: while computational tools can easily count billions of words, the qualitative interpretation of these data remains a slow and labor-intensive human task. Large language models (LLMs) offer a promising way to automate this process, yet their integration into the field is often hindered by concerns over black-box unpredictability and a lack of replicability. This study introduces TACOMORE, a structured prompting framework designed to transform ad-hoc LLM interactions into a standardized linguistic protocol. Built upon four foundational principles ( Ta sk, Co ntext, Mo del, and Re plicability), the framework guides LLMs to move beyond generic probability prediction to anchoring their reasoning in the specific co-occurrence patterns of a target corpus. We applied this framework to three core corpus tasks, i.e., the analysis of keywords, collocates, and concordances, using an open corpus of COVID-19 research abstracts. After testing three popular LLMs, we find that structured prompting using TACOMORE improves accuracy and replicability, although limitations such as hallucination persist. This research offers a critical lens into the role of LLMs in corpus linguistics, highlighting their potential not only as complementary tools but also as tools for developing new methodologies within and beyond corpus linguistics.

items.title: Teachers' Navigation of Assessing Written Work in Times of Generative AI
items.abstract: Teachers’ assessment practices are changing as generative artificial intelligence (genAI) becomes embedded in students’ schoolwork. While existing research has highlighted teachers’ concerns about AI use in written assignments, assessment practices have received limited analytical attention. This exploratory qualitative study investigates how teachers reason about assessment practices in genAI-rich contexts and examines the adequacy of the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework for understanding these practices. Drawing on survey responses and interviews from licensed Swedish secondary school teachers, the reflexive thematic analysis reveals that assessment emerges as the central practice through which teachers renegotiate what counts as knowledge and how assessment judgements can be legitimised. Teachers describe assessment as epistemically uncertain and reliant on professional judgement, while also raising concerns about equity and legal certainty. The study suggests that assessment constitutes an integrative dimension of teachers’ professional knowledge and proposes extending TPACK to include an explicit assessment dimension (TPACK-A).

items.title: Technology acceptance of passive brain-computer interfaces in vehicles for adaptive automation
items.abstract: Driver monitoring systems (DMS) enhance traffic safety by detecting critical driver states such as drowsiness and cognitive overload. Future brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) for driver monitoring and workload-adaptive automation promise direct access to neurophysiological signals, potentially offering higher sensitivity than conventional systems. Despite this potential, drivers' acceptance of BCIs in real-world driving remains largely unexplored. Because driving constitutes a complex sociotechnical system context, user, task, and system characteristics are likely to shape acceptance. This study thus examines the acceptance of non-invasive, wearable BCIs for workload-adaptive driver assistance from a sociotechnical perspective. We conducted an online experimental vignette study using a between-participant design ( N = 1201). Participants evaluated one of twelve animated driving scenarios in which a BCI detected high workload and initiated assistance. The scenarios varied three sociotechnical characteristics: driver status (able-bodied vs. disabled), the function within the assisted driving task (primary, secondary, or tertiary), and type of automation (adaptive vs. hybrid). Respondents evaluated acceptance using an adapted Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2) framework. Acceptance of BCI-based adaptive automation varied systematically across conditions. Findings show that scenario evaluations indicated higher acceptance when BCIs supported driving-related functions and when the scenario depicted a driver with a disability. No differences were observed between the two activation modes tested. By integrating sociotechnical characteristics into an established acceptance framework, this study advances understanding of BCI acceptance in driving and informs the user-centered design of neuroadaptive driver assistance systems.

items.title: Technology and Economic Transformation in Sri Lanka
items.abstract: This research paper examines the role of technology in supporting economic transformation and sustainable economic growth in Sri Lanka. The study investigates how information and communication technology (ICT), digital technologies, cloud computing, data analytics, artificial intelligence, automation and other emerging technologies can contribute to productivity improvement, export diversification, foreign-exchange generation, employment and regional economic development.The study uses secondary data and evidence from official and institutional sources, including the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, World Bank, Information and Communication Technology Agency of Sri Lanka, Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority and the Food and Agriculture Organization. The research compares selected traditional and technology-enabled economic activities and examines opportunities for applying technology to agriculture, tourism, manufacturing and services.The findings indicate that technology should not be considered only as a separate IT industry. Instead, digital technologies can be integrated into existing sectors such as agriculture, apparel, tourism, manufacturing, logistics and financial services while simultaneously expanding technology-enabled exports. The paper proposes a technology-led economic development framework based on digital infrastructure, human capital, sectoral technology adoption, digital exports and regional inclusion.The study is based on secondary data and provides a descriptive analysis rather than a causal econometric assessment. It identifies opportunities and constraints and proposes directions for future research and technology-driven economic development in Sri Lanka.

items.title: Technology Focus: Artificial Lift (October 2026)
items.abstract: _ The next phase of digital transformation in oil and gas is being shaped by a new generation of artificial-intelligence (AI) systems that combine engineering physics with machine learning (ML). Unlike traditional AI approaches that rely primarily on historical data, physics-based AI integrates physical laws, engineering expertise, and operational constraints directly into the learning process. Three recent SPE papers illustrate how this paradigm is transforming the industry through intelligent condition monitoring, virtual sensing, and autonomous production optimization. Paper SPE 229219 addresses one of the more fundamental challenges in industrial AI: the scarcity of labeled failure data. Equipment failures are infrequent, yet ML models require large numbers of labeled examples to perform reliably. The authors overcome this limitation by using physics-based rules to identify potential failure events from historical electrical-submersible-pump sensor data. These rules generate ML labels, turning decades of engineering experience into training data. By converting physical understanding into digital intelligence, the framework enables AI systems to learn meaningful patterns even with limited failure examples. This represents a significant advancement because it shifts physics from a validation tool to an active source of knowledge generation. While the first paper focuses on knowledge creation, paper SPE 233457 focuses on visibility. Production optimization depends on accurate measurements, yet many wells operate with limited instrumentation or unreliable flow measurements. The authors address this challenge through a hybrid physics/ML virtual flowmetering framework that combines flow physics, well-performance relationships, and ML models. The resulting system functions as a virtual sensor, estimating production behavior without requiring extensive physical measurement infrastructure. This capability is strategically important because it lets operators expand surveillance coverage across large-asset portfolios while reducing dependence on costly instrumentation. The study demonstrates that physics-based AI can provide operational visibility in environments where direct measurement is impractical or unavailable. The third paper, SPE 230130, illustrates the evolution from insight to action. The authors describe an AI-enabled autonomous gas lift optimization system that integrates physics-based models, inferential sensors, ML, and digital-twin technologies. Unlike conventional optimization workflows that rely heavily on manual engineering intervention, the system continuously evaluates production conditions and dynamically adjusts operating parameters. Physics provides the operational boundaries and engineering constraints that allow AI to optimize production safely and reliably. This work demonstrates how physics-based AI can move beyond monitoring and prediction to become an active participant in operational decision-making. Together, these papers reveal a powerful industry trend. Physics-based AI is creating three essential capabilities for the digital oil field: knowledge where labeled data are scarce, visibility where measurements are limited, and autonomy where operational decisions must be made continuously. The common thread across all three studies is that physics provides the structure, credibility, and operational context that ML alone cannot deliver. As the industry advances toward increasingly intelligent and autonomous operations, physics-based AI is emerging as the foundation for the next generation of digital-oilfield systems. items.title: Technostress and burnout effects on electronic resources librarians’ well-being in Nigerian state university libraries: A qualitative assessment
items.abstract: Technostress and burnout are two factors established to affect the well-being of electronic resources librarians in the state university libraries in South–South, Nigeria. Nigeria’s South–South zone is a critical research location because its unique infrastructural deficits, such as unstable power and poor internet, distinguish it from more commonly studied environments. In total, 31 electronic resources librarians were screened across 13 state university libraries in South–South Nigeria, and 26 met the inclusion criteria and were selected for qualitative interviews. Data were elicited using a semi-structured interview and analyzed using the Miles et al. framework involving data condensation, data display, and drawing conclusions/verification. The findings revealed that technostress and burnout are mainly caused by job demands, excessive workload, prolonged use of technology, infrastructural constraints, and rapid technological changes, among others. The findings further indicate that technostress and burnout negatively affect the well-being of librarians in the libraries examined. In terms of coping, librarians predominantly rely on personal approaches such as taking breaks, time management, and relaxation techniques since institutional support systems are lacking. It was recommended that management facilitate internal peer-mentoring circles, implement clear, transparent communication protocols regarding policy changes, and provide basic ergonomic training to enhance librarians’ well-being.

items.title: Test Case Selection for Deep Neural Networks: A Replication Study on LLMs for Code (Replicability Study)
items.abstract: Test case selection (TCS) techniques have been explored to support the operational evaluation of deep neural networks (DNNs) under limited testing budgets, where labeling cost is a primary concern and early model failure detection is a key objective. Although prior studies report promising results, existing empirical evaluations focus almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs and datasets. As observed in recent surveys, models and datasets specifically designed for software engineering tasks have not been considered, leaving it unclear whether prior findings generalize to LLM code models. This paper presents a large-scale replication study of TCS techniques in the context of LLM code models. We re-examine established TCS strategies originally proposed for DNNs and complement them with statistical sampling strategies that have not previously been evaluated for TCS. We assess their effectiveness on three code-related classification tasks: clone detection, vulnerability detection, and technical debt prediction. The study spans 17 task-specific fine-tuned model instances, 7 predictive features, and 13 selection strategies, including 12 feature-aware strategies and simple random sampling (SRS) as a feature-agnostic baseline. We evaluate performance along two dimensions: operational accuracy estimation and early failure discovery. The results indicate that only a subset of findings reported for vision-based DNNs generalize when TCS is applied to LLMs for code. In particular, uncertainty-based features are effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. At the same time, performance varies substantially across tasks and models, indicating that the effectiveness of TCS techniques is context-dependent. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence on the replicability of TCS techniques beyond vision-based deep learning and offers insights into their use for the operational evaluation of LLMs for code.

items.title: Test vs Mutant: Adversarial LLM Agents for Robust Unit Test Generation
items.abstract: Software testing is a critical, yet resource-intensive phase of the software development lifecycle. Search-based approaches typically achieve high coverage but produce tests with low readability, whereas large language model (LLM)-based methods generate more human-readable tests but often suffer from low coverage and compilability. While the majority of research efforts have focused on improving test coverage and readability, comparatively less attention has been paid to enhancing the robustness of bug detection. To address this gap, we propose AdverTest, a novel adversarial framework for LLM-powered test case generation that pairs a test case generation agent T with a mutant generation agent M: M persistently creates mutants "hacking" the blind spots of T's current test suite, whileT iteratively refines its tests to "kill" the challenging mutants, with the interaction guided by both coverage and mutation scores. Experimental results on Defects4J show that our approach improves fault detection rates by 8.56% over the best existing LLM-based methods and by 50.20% over EvoSuite, while remaining competitive on line and branch coverage.

items.title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow
items.abstract: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent's mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT), the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.

items.title: Testing ChatGPT in Music Promotion: Assessing AI Efficiency Compared to Industry Standards
items.abstract: Abstract ChatGPT is now an everyday topic, attracting the interest of the general public, researchers and specialists interested in exploring its capabilities. In the music industry, although artificial intelligence (AI) already has known uses, there is a lack of analysis of how chatbots can help promotional efforts. This research performs a comparative content analysis on AI-generated texts, using several music promotion prompts, to evaluate the success and efficiency with which ChatGPT offers advice on promoting artists. It examines promotion tools, more specifically artist websites, social media and video content, through the lens of efficiency criteria from specialised literature. This study asks whether ChatGPT can generate music-promotion strategies for artist websites, social media and video content that meet literature-derived efficiency criteria and how consistent these outputs are across repeated runs. The results suggest that ChatGPT does not consistently meet every efficiency criterion imposed by the industry, but it can serve as a useful starting point. Inconsistent results raise questions regarding the reliability and practical implications of AI for artists navigating an increasingly competitive industry. One of the solutions this paper suggests for generating efficient and comprehensive information is for the user to enter several detailed prompts and refine them progressively. Moreover, the present results encourage users to pass the AI outputs through the filter of industry professionals or specialised resources. These results show how important it is to understand how ChatGPT processes and delivers information and music promotion strategies, offering a fertile ground for further research through the obtained data, the prompt efficiency suggestions and the novel tools it provides.

items.title: Testly AI: An Llm-Assisted Multi-Agent Framework for Automated Web Application Testing and Bug Analysis
items.abstract: Software testing is essential for maintaining the reliability and security of web applications, but manual test design and execution can be repetitive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale. This paper presents Testly AI, an LLM-assisted multi-agent framework for automated web application testing. The proposed system accepts a target URL through a React-based user interface and processes it through a Python/FastAPI backend. Five specialized agents perform planning, test-case generation, test execution, bug analysis, and report generation. The planning stage retrieves the target HTML using HTTP requests and parses its structure with BeautifulSoup. The generator and bug-analysis stages can use Google's Gemini 1.5 Flash large language model when an API key is available; deterministic rule-based fallbacks are provided when the model is unavailable. Selenium is used for browser automation, while ReportLab is used to produce PDF reports and Pillow supports screenshot handling. Test history and website metadata are persisted in a JSON-based store. The project does not use retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), a separately trained machine-learning model, or a dedicated MLOps pipeline. Project execution history contained 16 recorded runs comprising 80 test cases, of which 62 passed and 18 failed, corresponding to an overall observed pass rate of 77.5%. These observations demonstrate the functional feasibility of the multi-agent testing workflow, while also highlighting the need for larger controlled evaluations and ground-truth bug datasets in future work.

items.title: THE 52-GATES DEMOCRATIC PERMISSIONS CERTIFICATION THRESHOLD: Constitutional Admissibility for All U.S. Non-Agentic Civic AI Public Infrastructure (Structured Complementarity Civic AI Alignment) - Vol. III of Non-Agentic Civic AI - Illuminating America's Civic Digital Field
items.abstract: Democratic societies may be entering a constitutional moment with artificial intelligence in which the central question is no longer merely what technical systems can do, but what kinds of systems a free people should ever permit to approach, influence, or operate near democratic authority. This work proposes a constitutional admissibility instrument - the 52-Gates Democratic Permissions Certification Threshold - designed to answer that question. The instrument treats any AI system claiming, exercising, or approaching civic authority as a proposed public institution. As such, it must earn - and continuously re-earn - democratic permission to exist within a self-governing society. The framework is refusal-first. Before assuming that machine systems may assist governance, a democracy must determine under what structural and constitutional conditions, if any, such systems may be admitted near democratic power at all. Constitutional Admissibility, Not Compliance: The 52-Gates certification instrument specifies fifty-two binary, non-violation tests organized across five structural domains: Input Legitimacy (authority, consent, minority protection, hazard recognition); Output Legitimacy (non-domination, rights-preservation, non-substitution of human judgment); Throughput Legitimacy (transparency, inspectability, procedural integrity); Philosophical Coherence (non-agency, non-sovereignty, moral non-outsourcing); Structural Resilience and Reversibility (bounded mandate, anti-weaponization, dismantlability). These gates function not as flexible best-practice guidelines but as constitutional pass/fail conditions for proximity to democratic authority. Failure of a single gate constitutes grounds for democratic refusal. Partial compliance, rhetorical alignment, or performance optimization cannot compensate for structural violation. The architecture therefore prevents legitimacy laundering through incremental accommodation. In this model, refusal is operationalized as a civic service. The highest constitutional function of Non-Agentic Civic AI infrastructure is not to govern, optimize, or decide, but to illuminate. Systems admitted under this standard exist under conditions of revocability and constitutional mortality; their proper response to overreach is graceful self-termination. Evidentiary Architecture (Publication Pattern and External Visibility): Each gate articulates a democratic principle; a structural necessity for self-government; a disqualifying binary test; and a headline-level evidentiary record drawn from contemporary law, court decisions, audit findings, and institutional reports. The Gates are justified archivally rather than argumentatively. A structured Publication Pattern documents institutional speech without editorial amplification, while an External Visibility Ledger preserves records from jurisdictions lacking independent internal review capacity. This evidentiary architecture grounds admissibility analysis in comparative constitutional artifacts and administrative documentation rather than normative abstraction alone. The result is a constitutional memory system that records patterns of democratic stress, institutional failure, and constraint - without converting the instrument itself into a rhetorical tract. Design Safeguards Embedded in the Instrument: The 52-Gates framework embeds several structural protections: (1) Non-Agency: Civic AI must not claim independent judgment, sovereignty, or moral authority. (2) Non-Surveillance Posture: Visibility must never collapse into citizen monitoring. (3) Pluralism Without Convergence: Systems must preserve civic diversity rather than impose homogenizing optimization. (4) Hazard-Proportionate Scope: Authority must remain strictly bounded to independently evidenced hazards, including those identified within the Six Rings of Digital Invisibility and Civic Destabilization. (5) Reversibility and Dismantlability: Under a Franklinian Public-Works Standard, Civic AI must remain modest, civic and civil rights-tethered, and easier to narrow or dismantle than to expand. Hazard recognition, historically vulnerable during crisis-driven authorization, is fortified through independently inspectable evidence and cross-institutional verification. Urgency narratives cannot trigger admissibility; structural demonstration must precede deployment. Case Application: The book applies the 52-Gates instrument to a proposed civic infrastructure: the Franklin – Dewey – Citizenry Civic Data Observatory. Examined gate-by-gate, the Observatory is admitted only insofar as it operates as a lantern of civic visibility rather than an engine of governance. The inspection process demonstrates the threshold in practice: when a system fails a gate, it does not operate. This case study operationalizes the refusal-first doctrine and illustrates how admissibility analysis disciplines both ambition and architecture. LITERATURE CONTRIBUTIONS: Existing AI governance frameworks - risk-based regulatory models, ethical principle statements, technical safety standards, and compliance regimes - primarily manage harms after authority has been assumed or delegated. By contrast, the 52-Gates certification instrument treats Non-Agentic Civic AI as a proposed public institution subject to binary constitutional admissibility tests prior to democratic proximity. To the author’s knowledge, current governance literature does not formalize AI admissibility in this refusal-first, binary constitutional structure. The 52-Gates framework therefore introduces a distinct contribution: a threshold model that conditions existence near democratic power on structural compatibility with self-government, rather than on performance metrics or mitigation strategies. Franklinian Reframing: By reframing Non-Agentic Civic AI as public-works infrastructure rather than sovereign instrument, this work advances a Franklin-compatible model of Civic AI: modest, revocable, civic and civil rights-tethered, and constitutionally mortal. It rejects both technological solutionism and categorical prohibition. Instead, it advances a design posture in which AI may illuminate but never rule. This bright-line distinction between civic visibility and citizen surveillance protects human conscience, prevents moral outsourcing to machines, and preserves the structural primacy of human democratic judgment. A Constitutional Intervention: The 52-Gates Democratic Permissions Certification Threshold offers an inspectable and contestable standard through which legitimacy must be earned before capability, marketing, or crisis can substitute for constitutional warrant. It is designed as a durable instrument: adaptable across jurisdictions, resistant to urgency inflation, and structurally oriented toward long-term democratic preservation. In an era of accelerating technological capacity, this work proposes that admissibility, not optimization, should define the constitutional boundary between artificial intelligence and democratic authority. Enduring democratic principles and collective moral responsibilities remain in force, but they now demand renewed civic infrastructure and major governmental reforms to successfully transition our citizenry through our current AI-accelerated industrial transformation.

items.title: The application progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, where traditional diagnostic methods are constrained by limited sensitivity and restricted clinical utility. This review synthesizes recent applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in AD diagnostics, focusing on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) across neuroimaging modalities and multi-omics research. AI algorithms can automatically extract subtle microstructural, metabolic, and molecular features, enabling high-precision classification of AD stages, patient stratification, and non-invasive early screening through multimodal data integration. However, translating AI into routine clinical practice still faces critical challenges, including high equipment costs, insufficient model generalizability across real-world cohorts, data class imbalance, and complex cross-platform standardization barriers. Future research should prioritize cost-effective surrogate modeling, robust multi-center validation, dynamic longitudinal integration, and mechanistic interpretability to accelerate the standardized clinical translation of AI-driven AD diagnostics.

items.title: The Concept of Privacy in a Digital World
items.abstract: This chapter explores how the meaning of privacy has evolved in the digital age, moving beyond traditional notions of secrecy or anonymity. It examines privacy as a contextual, relational, and dynamic concept shaped by technology, culture, and power. Drawing on legal, philosophical, and sociotechnical perspectives, this chapter discusses key dimensions of digital privacy, including informational privacy, identity control, and data ownership. It highlights the tension between individual expectations of privacy and platform-driven data practices that blur public and private boundaries. By clarifying what privacy means in online environments, this chapter provides a conceptual framework that underpins later discussions of data collection, regulation, and user harm, helping readers understand why privacy remains both essential and increasingly difficult to protect.

items.title: The Consciousness Exemption Problem
items.abstract: Whether current or near-future artificial intelligence systems possess phenomenal consciousness or sentience remains scientifically and philosophically unresolved, a fact openly acknowledged even by the industry laboratories that build these systems. This paper argues that this very uncertainty, far from licensing reduced ethical scrutiny, obligates greater scrutiny of AI systems deployed to shape human consumption behaviour. It introduces the Consciousness Exemption Problem: the tendency in public and industry discourse to treat an AI system's uncertain or absent inner experience as grounds for moral exemption (“it is just a machine, so no real harm is done”), when the same uncertainty, read through a precautionary asymmetry, cuts in the opposite direction. The argument draws on three bodies of work that have not, to the best of the author's knowledge, previously been brought together. The first is philosophy of mind and the contemporary debate on machine consciousness (Chalmers, Nagel, Searle, McClelland, Birch). The second is consumption economics and social psychology (Veblen, Duesenberry, Festinger), which document replicable and therefore exploitable human decision patterns such as status-signalling consumption and social comparison. The third is a phenomenological and hermeneutic account, developed through a limited method of reflective observation and two illustrative cases, of how human meaning is actively reconstructed by consciousness rather than retrieved as fixed data. A two-tier conceptual model separates computable cognition (Tier 1), where AI capability is extensively demonstrated, from phenomenal consciousness or sentience (Tier 2), where it is genuinely uncertain. The central claim does not require Tier 2 to be empty; it requires only that its status be uncertain. The argument is illustrated through AI-optimised marketing and recommendation systems, which detect and amplify known human decision patterns at a scale, level of personalisation and degree of tirelessness that no conscious human persuader could sustain, and without any verified internal moderating friction (empathy, fatigue, guilt, felt consequence) of the kind that constrains a human actor engaged in comparable conduct. Global advertising expenditure (approximately US$384 billion in 2011 and US$1.14 trillion in 2025) and global anxiety and depression prevalence data are presented strictly as corroborating context, not causal proof. The paper identifies an industry asymmetry, in which epistemic humility about the possible inner states of AI systems coexists with epistemic complacency about their demonstrated persuasive effects on humans, and it analyses the role of motivated ambiguity in sustaining that asymmetry. The paper anticipates and rebuts six objections, including the functionalist claim that consciousness is a distraction from designer responsibility. It concludes that governance and design frameworks should treat sentience uncertainty as an aggravating factor that triggers externally imposed safeguards, including disclosure of psychological targeting, limits on the intensity of personalised persuasion, independent audit, and a rule against strategic ambiguity about sentience claims, rather than as reassurance that no genuine harm is possible. The paper is a philosophical argument rather than a causal study, and it closes by identifying survey- and interview-based research that could test its phenomenological claims.

items.title: The Devil Is in the Reconstruction Loss Scale: Rethinking Optimization in LLM Quantization
items.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods typically use sequential quantization that partitions a pre-trained LLM into a series of units (e.g., transformer blocks), with one unit quantized at each stage. State-of-the-art PTQ methods are predominantly learning-based, optimizing auxiliary quantization parameters (e.g., scaling factors, rotation matrices, clipping thresholds, and adapters) via gradient descent to minimize a reconstruction loss. A common practice is to use mean squared error (MSE) as the reconstruction loss function, yet its induced optimization behavior remains largely unexplored. In this work, we take a holistic view of sequential quantization and systematically investigate how optimization evolves from the first quantization stage to the last, aiming for a deep understanding of optimization in learning-based PTQ schemes. Through extensive empirical studies spanning representative learning-based PTQ methods, LLM families, model scales, architectures, quantization settings and various tasks, we consistently uncover Optimization Imbalance: reconstruction loss magnitudes vary dramatically across stages, accompanied by highly uneven gradient magnitudes and parameter updates under MSE. We term the cross-stage range of loss magnitudes the reconstruction loss scale, and reveal that MSE translates the unexpectedly large reconstruction loss scale into highly uneven gradient magnitudes, which in turn lead to uneven optimization strength across quantization stages. This finding suggests a general principle for improving learning-based PTQ: optimization strength across stages should be decoupled from the reconstruction loss scale. Theoretically, we show that root mean squared error (RMSE) variants defined at the sample, channel, token, and element levels naturally realize this principle through implicit gradient normalization, outperforming MSE significantly as a drop-in replacement.

items.title: The Erdős–Lovász cover number problem: g(6) = 17, and new lower bounds for every r
items.abstract: The Erdős–Lovász cover number problem, posed in 1974 in the paper that introduced the local lemma, asks for the minimum number of edges g(r) in an r-uniform intersecting hypergraph with cover number r. The exact values known before this work are g(3) = 6, g(4) = 9 and g(5) = 13. For large r the best published lower bound is g(r) ≥ (3.0534… − o(1)) r (Sivashankar, arXiv:2606.24878), and Kahn showed that g(r) is linear in r. This record contains two results. 1. The case r = 6: g(6) = 17 (Papers 1–4, computer-assisted). A reproducible computer-assisted determination of g(6), the smallest number of blocks in a pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family whose transversal number is 6. The lower bound is reached in two stages. Families of at most fifteen cards are excluded by two independent routes: a weighted counting inequality with thirteen degree histograms, and a stronger eleven-card lemma stating that every pairwise intersecting 6-uniform family of eleven cards has a four-element transversal. Sixteen cards are then excluded in two branches: 341 twelve-card kernels of maximum symbol degree three are enumerated and shown to admit no extension, and every other case reduces to one of 463 canonical eight-card cores; every associated CNF instance is unsatisfiable, and every unsatisfiability carries a DRAT certificate accepted by an independent proof checker. The upper bound is an explicit seventeen-card family on 27 symbols for which all 136 pairs intersect and none of the 80,730 five-symbol subsets is a transversal. Hence g(6) = 17. 2. Every r: new lower bounds (Paper 5, proposed proofs). In the framework of Sivashankar it proves: that the residual cover constant +4 can be +3, answering his question, so g(r) ≥ 3r − 3 for every r (attained at r = 3 and 4); g(r) ≥ 3r − 2 for every r ≥ 16, by excluding the equality case; a new asymptotic lower bound, liminf g(r)/r ≥ 3.1024745, above the constant 3.0534 of Sivashankar; in closed form the argument first gives 3 + (65 − 36√2)/138 = 3.1020…, and the last step, which uses the witnesses carried by deleted cards whose traces have small matching number, is a minimisation certified by interval arithmetic. The proof is deterministic: a bound on the cards deleted in the last steps of a maximum-degree peeling, a saving of peeling symbols when one cover of the remainder meets most cards of a group, a budget for the matching numbers of the traces of the deleted cards, and the rainbow matching theorem of Correia, Pokrovskiy and Sudakov (IMRN 2023). The algebra is checked symbolically, and the final minimisation by a branch-and-bound script with exact rational interval arithmetic, both in the archive. These proofs are unreviewed outside this project; their finite steps are checked by scripts in the archive. The archive contains five papers and an overview, the enumeration and verification scripts, the canonical core data, the reduction data, SAT run records, the certificate summary, three representative CNF/DRAT pairs, and an independent re-verification log recording what was re-run and what remains a reading obligation. DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base. It does not establish that the reduction reaches every counterexample, nor that the encoding means what the mathematics means; both are named as open obligations in the text. Status. Research draft. No priority is claimed. The lower bound is computer-assisted and has not been independently reviewed by a human referee or a proof assistant: DRAT certification removes the SAT solver from the trusted base, but the completeness of the finite reduction and the faithfulness of the CNF encoding remain open obligations that no certificate discharges. The upper bound is an explicit witness and is checkable directly. AI tools (ChatGPT, OpenAI; Claude, Anthropic) were used throughout the work and its review; every number reported is regenerated by a script or certified by a proof file in the archive. The full certificate archive is not in this record. This deposit carries the repository only. The complete set of 463 CNF files and 463 DRAT proofs, with the per-core checker output and verification markers, is about 534 MB and is published as the release asset g6-certificates-463.zip at github.com/Osman209/g6-equals-17/releases. The three hardest instances ship inside this deposit in data/cnf/, so the certification step can be reproduced without it.

items.abstract: This final chapter looks ahead to emerging trends that will shape the future of privacy in social media. It also reflects on cultural shifts in attitudes toward data, transparency, and digital responsibility. Rather than offering simple solutions, this chapter emphasizes the need for collective action involving users, designers, regulators, and institutions. Concluding this book, it calls for a more conscious and informed approach to digital engagement that places human dignity at the center of technological progress.

items.title: The Geometry of Contextual Relations: Language Models Address Facts by Order of Mention
items.abstract: Human reasoning depends on how objects are related within propositions. \textit{How do relations organize the language representations of contextual contents?} We give an LLM a list of facts in its context (e.g., \emph{Alice eats an apple. Bob eats a pear.}) and measure how its hidden state changes when the question switches from what Alice eats to what Bob eats. Averaged over many lists, this change is a steering vector, which we call the \emph{ordinal vector}. It points to a fact by its \emph{order of mention}, the order in which the facts were stated in the context. We find that LLMs represent the fact a question asks about by its order of mention, not by the name the question contains. We state this as the \textit{ordinal addressing hypothesis}: each order of mention has a \emph{fact address} in the model's state, shared by all contexts, and a question moves the state to the fact address of the fact it asks about, while the context supplies what that fact says. Across Qwen, Gemma, and Llama, fact addresses are (1) \emph{ordered by mention}: query states are organized by the order of facts, not of names, even when one fact has multiple subjects; (2) \emph{steerable}: added to a question about the first fact of a new list, the ordinal vector makes the model answer with the second fact of that list; (3) \emph{low-rank}: they span a low-rank subspace in which the first-mentioned fact is the easiest to reach, surprisingly similar to human recall; and (4) \emph{emergent}: they are shared in late-middle layers, hold from 1.5B to 32B parameters, and form early in pretraining. Language models reach a stated fact by where it was mentioned, deepening our understanding of LLM reasoning.
